articles.text: Casting votes for Thomasson, Medhekar Editor: I would like to enthusiastically endorse Ruchi Medhekar and Lindsay Thomasson for the two open seats on PUSD’s School Board. I’ve gotten to know Lindsay and Ruchi very well in the last few years, and among the many things I admire about them is that they show up and do the hard work. As someone who has attended nearly every School Board meeting since June 2020, I am routinely struck by how much time and effort it takes to be a truly engaged School Board member. Our School Board members are unpaid, but they spend hours and hours every week researching upcoming meeting topics, attending the bi-weekly School Board meetings (which often run 4+ hours), and participating in numerous school and community committees. I am fully confident that Lindsay and Ruchi will not only accomplish the many tasks and responsibilities required of successful School Board members, but they will throw themselves into those roles with the same energy and passion that they’ve already brought to this district in their previous volunteer work. Those roles include assuming the parent club presidencies during (arguably) the most difficult school year in the history of this district – 2020/2021 when we were in the throes of Covid and emotions were running very high among all district stakeholders. Lindsay and Ruchi were able to use their positions as parent club presidents to advocate for the needs of students – many of whom were struggling sigduring that difficult period have only strengthened since then, and I know will serve them well as they continue to build bridges throughout our community as School Board members. In addition to their parent club presidencies, Lindsay and Ruchi have stepped up to do the work on less visible but arguably even more impactful committees like being site council representatives, where they work with school principals to plan for the needs of their school; working on the LCAP committee, where they advocated for a district-wide survey earlier this year to ensure that the current LCAP goals reflect the priorities of the community. Additionally, Ruchi has served on the board of the Piedmont Education Foundation to better understand the ways our dollars are spent in this district, and on the Piedmont Recreation sub-committee, where she has routinely advocated for working parents struggling to find childcare in the city’s afterschool program. Lindsay has served on the Superintendent Advisory Committee, where she has had a direct line to our district leadership and has passionately advocated for improvements to our literacy curriculum, and she co-leads the Wellness Center Support Committee, where she works to raise money to support our students’ social and emotional needs. This is the kind of hard work and dedication that being a successful School Board member requires. We need School Board members willing to dig in and devote their time and energy to the work. articles.text: Last week I read a letter to the editor from “ new neighbor,” Tu Ngoc Nguyen, who stated that the PiedmontVotes.com website had created a smear campaign against school board candidate Shirley Hooi. I opened PiedmontVotes.com and ironically the “smear campaign” is composed of words Ms. Hooi used in her multiple letters to the editor and commentaries she wrote to the Piedmont Post. The core of her opinions came down to PUSD staying in their lane and not teaching anything about critical race theory, racial oppression or related material that would run the risk of her mixed race children feeling white guilt or questioning her white husband’s beliefs towards people of color. Tu Ngoc Nguyen then went on to bash Piedmont Racial Equity Campaign for their perceived part in the PiedmontVotes.com profile and how they were targeting the only Asian American candidate. That opinion is clearly debunked on PREC’s facebook page. [An example of] racial bias from teachers came when my black son was encouraged to “aim lower” for his academic goals in his first year in Piedmont. That same son was stopped 10 years later for the audacity of walking while black (200 yards from my front door) in a community policing encounter by two officers of color. (PPD was swift to respond, held two separate meetings with me and my son and admitted to racial bias being present across all races of peace officers, and antibias training was mandated by Chief Bowers.) It was a best-case scenario and radically different from police encounters in other neighborhoods that we have witnessed via our media. Please vote for the candidates who understand the importance of educating our children about our past mistakes as a country. articles.text: This week marks the 25th anniversary of the Piedmont Post. It’s first edition was 12 pages and hardly offered any promise, let alone optimism, that it might be around a quarter century later. In a small town with only a few commercial businesses, the outlook for its survival was somewhat bleak. And then we began reading stories in the New York Times about the escalating number of local newspapers going out of business – over 2,000 at last count. And yet here we are – thriving and finding ways to thank the residents for so strongly supporting The Little Newspaper That Could. Over the next several weeks, you will read comments of some of the people who were there at the beginning – the optimists and pessimists. my core belief that the Post had taken its place in that long line referred to as the Fourth Estate which defines our democracy and the First Amendment, It would be not only essential to the vitality of our city government but would be a means to inform the community about a broad spectrum of “news” and opinion, and a forum for information and debate. I have always preferred ink on paper, loved holding a newspaper in my hands, even relishing its smell. And here it was, the Post, the first of many to come. Finally, let me say that the denizens of Piedmont should take pride in this weekly paper, for without their generous support it would not have flourished, grown in the number of pages (including color), and, in keeping with the times, is now available online. Without a doubt, after twenty-five years, week after week, it has become an integral part of the Piedmont community. May it continue for another quarter of a century. Chris Honore’ is the Post’s movie reviewer with occasional pieces on the Opinion page. He is married to Judi Honore’ and lives in Ashland, Oregon. license plate readers. I’m remembering bringing the Piedmont Post with us on vacation, then not remembering to send in the photo of us reading it. And now we see the names of people who were in school with our kid, and who are now running the city. Remembrances of the early days of the Piedmont Post, give way to the bigger picture – why it’s important to have a hometown newspaper. It’s not just to read about your kid, the activities of the community and local politics. It’s reading about the issues and challenges facing our town, some which seem to have stayed the same over 25 years. It keeps us up to date on the city and schools, and reminds us it’s important to be an active member of the community. As the Post has grown from 12 pages to 32 pages, it has not only survived, but prospered, maybe even beyond Gray’s initial vision. I’ve said to him that the Post is the only paper I know that’s growing instead of shrinking. I’d like to thank him and the Post for unwavering support of Piedmont, of the school fundraisers and other philanthropic community events. The Post has been an important voice for our community. Congratulations and thanks. Here’s to the next 25 years. Cheers! Sheryl and Bob Wong Manor Drive

The last four years have proven to be a busy time for Edel. In 2018 she gave the keynote address at OLLI and to the League of Women Voters in Piedmont on The State of US-Russian Relations. One year later she delivered talks at the Commonwealth Club in San Francisco, the University of Washington, and Berkeley City Club. Due in part to the publicity generated by op ed pieces she wrote for the New York Times between February and May this year, she was an invited commentator on CNN, MSNBC and Bay Area NBC. articles.text: On a fall morning, twenty-five years ago, Gray Cathrall and I sat in a Montclair coffee shop and he shared with me his vision for a hometown newspaper. He hoped to create a publication focused just on the news unique to this small tree-lined community, a paper that would give emphasis to the families that define Piedmont. At the time, I thought that Gray’s idea was more than doable, and I immediately signed on. Of course, there were caveats: neither of us were certain that a weekly paper was sustainable, and Gray pointed out that for the Piedmont Post – a perfect name – to survive it would have to rely on local subscriptions since there were few commercial advertisers available. But Gray was convinced that the town would not only see the value in a local paper, but they would step forward and embrace it as subscribers and underwriters. His enthusiasm and conviction were catching and the longer we talked the more I wanted to put pen to paper, so to speak. There was news to be told, school sports to be covered, and stories/reviews to be shared. pages.text: Wednesday, October 26, 2022 3 Happy 25th Anniversary Piedmont Post This week marks the 25th anniversary of the Piedmont Post. It’s first edition was 12 pages and hardly offered any promise, let alone optimism, that it might be around a quarter century later. In a small town with only a few commercial businesses, the outlook for its survival was somewhat bleak. And then we began reading stories in the New York Times about the escalating number of local newspapers going out of business – over 2,000 at last count. And yet here we are – thriving and finding ways to thank the residents for so strongly supporting The Little Newspaper That Could. Over the next several weeks, you will read comments of some of the people who were there at the beginning – the optimists and pessimists. The Post – 25 Years and counting By Chris Honoré On a fall morning, twenty-five years ago, Gray Cathrall and I sat in a Montclair coffee shop and he shared with me his vision for a hometown newspaper. He hoped to create a publication focused just on the news unique to this small tree-lined community, a paper that would give emphasis to the families that define Piedmont. At the time, I thought that Gray’s idea was more than doable, and I immediately signed on. Of course, there were caveats: neither of us were certain that a weekly paper was sustainable, and Gray pointed out that for the Piedmont Post – a perfect name – to survive it would have to rely on local subscriptions since there were few commercial advertisers available. But Gray was convinced that the town would not only see the value in a local paper, but they would step forward and embrace it as subscribers and underwriters. His enthusiasm and conviction were catching and the longer we talked the more I wanted to put pen to paper, so to speak. There was news to be told, school sports to be covered, and stories/reviews to be shared. And when the first edition of the Post actually appeared on October 20, 1998 – right in the middle of the high school football season – I was more than encouraged. It was a rush, and I recall writing a brief sidebar expressing my core belief that the Post had taken its place in that long line referred to as the Fourth Estate which defines our democracy and the First Amendment, It would be not only essential to the vitality of our city government but would be a means to inform the community about a broad spectrum of “news” and opinion, and a forum for information and debate. I have always preferred ink on paper, loved holding a newspaper in my hands, even relishing its smell. And here it was, the Post, the first of many to come. Finally, let me say that the denizens of Piedmont should take pride in this weekly paper, for without their generous support it would not have flourished, grown in the number of pages (including color), and, in keeping with the times, is now available online. Without a doubt, after twenty-five years, week after week, it has become an integral part of the Piedmont community. May it continue for another quarter of a century. Chris Honore’ is the Post’s movie reviewer with occasional pieces on the Opinion page. He is married to Judi Honore’ and lives in Ashland, Oregon. Unwavering support of the City for 25 years Editor: As I think back to October 1998 when the Post was founded, I had forgotten that our son had already graduated from Piedmont High. I had always connected his high school years with the Post. Those of us who were early “crowdfunders” for the Post were taking a leap of faith. I don’t think I’ve ever really thought of us as “subscribers” of the newspaper. My 25 years of memories include: Reading the PPD Blue every week, despite being one of the silly skunk entries. Noticing how the PPD Blue has more serious crimes now, including the weekly count of catalytic converter thefts and responses to license plate readers. I’m remembering bringing the Piedmont Post with us on vacation, then not remembering to send in the photo of us reading it. And now we see the names of people who were in school with our kid, and who are now running the city. Remembrances of the early days of the Piedmont Post, give way to the bigger picture – why it’s important to have a hometown newspaper. It’s not just to read about your kid, the activities of the community and local politics. It’s reading about the issues and challenges facing our town, some which seem to have stayed the same over 25 years. It keeps us up to date on the city and schools, and reminds us it’s important to be an active member of the community. As the Post has grown from 12 pages to 32 pages, it has not only survived, but prospered, maybe even beyond Gray’s initial vision. I’ve said to him that the Post is the only paper I know that’s growing instead of shrinking. I’d like to thank him and the Post for unwavering support of Piedmont, of the school fundraisers and other philanthropic community events. The Post has been an important voice for our community. Congratulations and thanks. Here’s to the next 25 years. Cheers! Sheryl and Bob Wong Manor Drive Let the politicians speak Editor: From the outset in 1998, the Post committed to cover the topics people wanted to read about: great coverage of youth sports, school events and community activities. More print about the things that make Piedmont a great place to live. More kids and people. Less coverage of the Mayors! The likely reason is that it has grown to more than 30 pages. Congratulations. articles.text: The Alameda County Registrar of Voters is seeking poll workers for the November 8, 2022 election. Poll workers play a critical role in making voting accessible to all community members – and get paid to do it. Workers are needed throughout Alameda County from Saturday, November 5 through Tuesday, November 8, election day. Interested community members can sign up online to volunteer at acgov.org/rovform_app/ewapply. The application is simple and takes just a few minutes to complete. Job details Poll workers are paid volunteers who perform tasks including: • Setting up and closing a polling place • Helping voters understand their rights • Protecting ballots and voting equipment The County Registrar of Voters office provides training for poll workers. Individuals are paid for training and time served as a poll worker. No special skills are required to be a poll worker. Eligibility requirements: • Must be a registered voter in California • Must be a legal permanent resident or green card holder • An eligible high school student Bilingual Poll Workers Sought Bilingual poll workers are especially needed. In Alameda County, assistance is provided to voters in Burmese, Chinese, Hindi, Khmer, Korean, Laotian, Mien, Mongolian, Punjabi, Spanish, Tagalog, Telugu, and Vietnamese. Residents fluent in any of these languages are urged to consider volunteering. Interested residents can find more information about volunteering as a poll worker at acvote.org/community/become-anelection-worker or by calling the Alameda County Registrar of Voters office at 510-272-6973.

articles.text: Big educational changes are coming to PUSD. The agenda for the day lists seven lecture hours on DEIB (Diversity, Equity, Inclusion, and Belonging) topics. No time was allocated for certified teachers about issues with dyslexia, academics, filling the student knowledge gap from the COVID era, or school safety. Also this month, the Piedmont Middle School presented a video to all its students about why grade achievement isn’t that important – a video intended for parents. During the first week of school, at least one of the 2nd grade teachers instructed children on being able to change their pronouns at any time. DEIB has a place in academics, but it seems quite imbalanced now. See for yourself at the school board meeting at 7 p.m. tonight. PUSD’s values, mission, and vision are in the process of being redefined. A progress report on PUSD’s educational action plan will be presented.

Do not put branches in the street, even small branches! They damage the street sweeping equipment. 2. Do not sweep debris from your yard into the gutter – sweep only leaves that fall naturally into the street. 3. Sweep leaves into narrow rows outside the flow line of the gutter. Do not put them in piles. The street sweepers cannot pick up piles of leaves effectively. 4. If you want to rake your leaves, you can now add them to your weekly unlimited green waste cart. articles.text: The biggest family camp of the year for Piedmont Scouts took place at Bort Meadow last weekend with the Cub Scout Overnighter and Webeloree. “This is an important event for our council,” explained Scout Executive Kate Benson. “Our Scouts BSA troops, Piedmont Community Service Crew, and Order of the Arrow do a great job supporting this overnighter for our younger Scouts. It’s one of the few events where all the programs weave together.” A total of 90 Cub Scouts and parents landed at the campground in Chabot Regional Park on Friday evening, ready for adventure. They selected their campsites, set up their tents, and played at full speed in the fading light. The Order of the Arrow – an honor society for Scouts BSA – arrived to make dinner for everyone before leading a campfire program. By 8:30 p.m., the Cubs were ready for bed and crawled into their sleeping bags for a night outdoors. They awoke Saturday morning to a continental breakfast and headed out for a one-mile hike. “This was the best part,” said one Cub during their roses-andthorns debrief. “I wanted to keep going.” As the younger Cubs packed up their tents and headed home, the older Cubs arrived on Saturday for their Webeloree. They started the day with a three-mile hike and set up camp upon their return. Piedmont Community Service Crew – a Venturing unit – showed up with lunch organized by Theo Ferguson. Webelos and their parents dined on pulled pork sandwiches, mac and cheese, fruit salad, chips, and banana boats cooked over hot coals. “Theo did an excellent job organizing the lunch,” said PCSC Crew advisor Ken Li. “The marshmallows and chocolate were tasty and sticky!” enthused several Webelos. Afternoon activities for the Webelos included first aid, knot skills, flag practice, and an engineering adventure. Scouts Samantha Pell and Madeleine Poon of Troop 1 led the First Aid section, walking the Webelos through the correct response for nose bleeds, hypothermia, abrasions, and more. articles.text: Tennis team beats Alameda, Castro Valley, St. Mary’s In a triumphant week, the Piedmont tennis team walking away with three victories in as many days including a pair of Western Alameda County Conference foes. They defeated Alameda narrowly 4-3 on the Hornets’ home courts on Thursday, October 20, beat St. Mary’s 6-1 the previous day, and bashed Castro Valley 6-1 at home on Tuesday, October 18. The most critical match was with Alameda, which had an opportunity to prevent the Highlanders from claiming a league championship outright. But the 4-3 victory kept Piedmont undefeated and on track for its first WACC crown since 2018. Matches remain against Berkeley and Bishop O’Dowd. The team is now 14-3 overall and a perfect 10-0 in league. An undefeated league season would be a return to tradition for the Highlanders’ girls’ tennis program, which went undefeated in league matches for 19 years, a state record. Thursday’s match with the Hornets wasn’t settled until Carolina Romanczuk at No. 3 singles defeating Allison Quan in three sets, 6-4, 3-6, 6-3. “The whole team is incredibly excited. We’re running a really good lineup this year with a good attitude, and I think that’s what’s going to push us through league,” said Romanczuk after her critical win. Trailing 4-1 in the first set, she won the next five games to win the set. She also won five straight games in the third set after trailing 3-1. “When I was down 3-1, I was just thinking back to my first set and how I was down 4-1. I was just pushing through and taking it one point at a time. I was just taking deep breathes and thinking of, not even about my own match, but just thinking about my team and trying to win it for my team,” said Romanczuk. 4-3 win over Alameda Against the Hornets, No. 1 singles starter Tanya Kononova won the first match of the day handily, 6-2, 6-4. Soon after, the No. 3 doubles team of Kate Jumper and Arianna Kortum won 6-3, 6-2, while Emma Eisemon and Cecilia DeFazio won 6-4, 7-6 (6-4) at No. 2 doubles to put PHS up 3-0, one win away from clinching the match. At No. 1 doubles, Mara LaForte and Michaela Bini lost a 5-set barnburner, 6-3, 5-7, 7-6 (7-5), and soon after, Annika Gilliland lost 6-3, 6-1 at the No. 4 singles spot. Suddenly the match was tied at 3-3. Romanczuk vs. Quan at the No. 3 singles was a long match, with each set highly contested. Romanczuk fell behind 4-1 in the first set disadvantage but pulled off a remarkable rally by winning five games in a row for a 6-4 victory. In the clinching third set, she also won five straight games to win 6-3. Her match featured several long rallies and Quan couldn’t maintain the same consistency as Romanczuk. However, Anne Jumper lost 6-3, 6-1 at the No. 2 singles spot. articles.text: Piedmont’s volleyball team had its season come to an end on Wednesday, October 19 at San Leandro with a victory in three sets, 25-11, 27-25, 25-23. “Just having the team come together and having them focus on team and personal goals. Just reminding that throughout the set of what they can do. It was a really close game; San Leandro’s effort on that side was why it was as close as it was. It was a lot of fun to watch,” said coach Mariah Cardenas. Piedmont compiled a record of 10-14 overall and 4-8 in league, and in spite of the record, marked an improvement from last year when the Highlanders finished 3-12 overall. “I wasn’t with the team last year, but I was around the team. They only won a few games throughout the season, we didn’t have a lot of different players, so it was a huge stride,” sad Cardenas. It marked the final appearance for seniors Bree DeYoung, Lila Town, Tara Kothari, Shelby Cavenaugh, and Eden Lorin. “This year, we have a lot of juniors who got experience. Last year was a building for us and we got to put more pieces into play this year,” said Lorin. In the wake of the Class of 2023, Piedmont will move ahead with players Izzy Grimmer, Maddy Mullin, Elena Stevens, Bauer and Beck Peterson, Molly Wagener, Klara Zietlow and leading outside hitter Sadie Town. “A lot of our seniors are important, so it’ll be interesting to see how their spots get filled up and what the coaches decide. But I’m excited, it’ll be good,” said Town. The runs included three aces by Lila Town and kills by Sadie Town, Kothari, Bauer Peterson. DeYoung closed out the set with a block to win 25-11. Photo by Korte Lee Eden Lorin had six kills and two serving aces in her final appearance at Piedmont. In the second set, San Leandro led 6-5 but conceded six straight points for PHS to lead 11-6. But from there, PHS pulled ahead 24-23 with a kill by Lorin and ace by Sadie Town to gain set point, but SL tied 25-25. Piedmont closed with the next two points due to an attacking and defensive error by the Pirates. In the final set, PHS battled to a 9-7 lead after starting out in a 4-1 deficit, but San Leandro briefly regained the lead at 10-9. From there, Piedmont scored eight of the next 12 points to lead 18-14. After a few points by San Leandro, PHS scored five of the next eight to lead 23-20. The Pirates battled to a one-point deficit at 24-23, but Cavenaugh killed the game with a mighty spike. Final stats include: Lorin with six kills and two aces. articles.text: The Chamber Music Society of San Francisco will perform a concert at the Piedmont Center for the Arts this Sunday afternoon, October 30, at 1:30 p.m. Tickets are available at: https:// bit.ly/3TpKMUZ. The quartet of Natasha Makhijani, Jory Fankuchen, Samsun van Loon, and Clio Tilton opens its 10th anniversary season with a return to Beethoven’s Opus 132, the masterpiece that brought these fine musicians together a decade ago. Beethoven’s String Quartet in A minor, opus 132, is from his collection of “late” quartets, written in the final years of his life. In these works, Beethoven turned inward, leaving us with some of his most exquisite and transcendental music. The quartet will also perform Caroline Shaw’s Valencia, and Mozart’s “Dissonance” String Quartet in C Major, K465. The Chamber Music Society of San Francisco is dedicated to bringing chamber music masterworks to diverse audiences. CMS of SF is passionate about concertizing in intimate settings, creating close connections between performers and listeners, and cultivating a relationship between music and audiences that extends far beyond the perimeter of the concert hall. Drawing listeners into the lives of the composers and the world of the music, CMS of SF concerts are a favorite destination for both chamber music lovers and those new to the genre. Members of CMS of SF can be heard performing with San Francisco Symphony, SF Opera, SF Ballet, San Francisco and New Century Chamber Orchestras, American Bach Soloists, Oakland Symphony and many others. The four founding members came together through their mutual love of the late Beethoven String Quartets. Collaborations have included artists such as Kay Stern, Stephen Prutsman, Jean-Michel Fonteneau, and Jodi Levitz. Trumpet soloist Pacho Flores will accompanies the symphony. To purchase tickets visit www. sfsymphony.org/dia, or call the box office at (415) 864-6000. Tickets are half off for children and young adults under the age of 18.

articles.text: Jason Klein, conductor of the Saratoga Symphony Babe Ruth made more money than the President of the United States. When a journalist asked him how he could justify that, the Babe said simply: “I had a better year than the president.“ Things have certainly changed since then. Salaries earned by big-name sports personalities are in the millions. But in the 1800s, it was the opera singers and classical musicians who made the millions, not sports figures. The great opera singer Jenny Lind made more money than anybody else. Her manager was “the great showman” PT Barnum. It is interesting to note that she demanded her money in advance – before she sang a note. The date was 1850. In 1905 the popular violinist Jan Kubelik made $500,000 in one season in the U.S. Compare that with the peanuts major league baseball players were paid. It is also interesting to note that at that time there was no difference between what we call “pop music“ and classical music. The public flocked to the classical music concerts. The most popular composer of the era was Stephen Foster, whose music was popular all over the world and was translated into many languages. It is sad to note that Stephen Foster died completely destitute. He needed a good lawyer. Food on the music trail If you take a short holiday trip to the Mother Lode in California, you can relive some of those exciting days of yore. You can visit the town of Jenny Lind, named for the great opera singer. Curiously she never came to California. It doesn’t matter where you go – all the towns are interesting and you can find good food everywhere. Be sure to go to the antique shops. Antique jewelry is almost always at bargain prices. Here is another tip: Get off the main street and go to some of the side streets and the back streets. Look at the architecture. Imagine yourself living during those heady days of the 19th Century and early 20th Century. Honor to Ukraine Last Sunday my wife and I went south to hear the Saratoga Symphony conducted by Jason Klein. I have always appreciated the conducting of Dr. Klein. He is a perfect example of an orchestra conductor inspiring his orchestra to play above their ability. In addition, his pre-concert words are not only informative, but they are very amusing. The concert was entitled “Honor to Ukraine”. Dr. Klein explained everything in his inimitable way. Four Ukrainian national composers were featured on the program. Three of them were virtually unknown to this critic, and the orchestra played in inspiring fashion. A piano concerto by Sergei Bortkiewicz featured dynamic playing by pianist Ron Brickman. It was like Rachmaninoff with shades of Wagner. In addition, there was a real swagger to the music. The result was invigorating. All in all, it was a unique program featuring a fine orchestra, a dynamic pianist and a superlative conductor. Some fan mail for Center for the Arts Last week a number of Piedmont residents told me how much they appreciate everything at the Piedmont Center for the Arts. You can’t beat the admission price, AND they frequently feed you. You can always find a parking space. And the quality of the entertainment is fantastic. Art included.

articles.text: Youth Musical Theater Company (YMTC) opens its 18th season with Matilda the Musical, with performances November 4–13 at the Malonga Casquelourd Center for the Arts in downtown Oakland. Roald Dahl’s beloved story of an extraordinary little girl is brought to dazzling, high-energy, and hilarious life in Matilda the Musical. Overlooked and unloved by her parents and bullied at school by the cruel Headmistress Trunchbull, 6-year-old genius Matilda finds solace in stories – in the pages of the books she devours and the tales that come tumbling out of her mind. With the help of a vivid imagination, her kind teacher Miss Honey, and an army of rebellious schoolchildren, Matilda decides to change her own story and rewrite her destiny. Matilda the Musical pays perfect tribute to the absurd humor and profound heart of Roald Dahl’s original story. The book was written by internationally acclaimed playwright Dennis Kelly, and the music and lyrics by Tim Minchin (Groundhog Day the Musical). Matilda premiered in the UK in 2011 and on Broadway in 2013, winning five Tony Awards, as well as more than 50 international awards, including the Olivier for Best New Musical. The show features a cast of 26 student performers and five apprentices (ages 12–18) from cities throughout the Bay Area. Dahlia Saffouri, a 10th grader at Piedmont High School, plays the role of a “Big Kid” and is the understudy for Mrs. Wormwood. They are led by a team of professional directors, designers, and musicians, including Directors Jennifer Boesing and Celeste Kamiya, Music Directors Diana Lee and Eric Walton, and Choreographer Nicole Helfer. The production features an 11-piece orchestra playing the original musical score. Matilda opens Friday November 4, with 7:30 p.m. performances on November 4-5 and November 11-12). Two matinee performances at 2 p.m. are scheduled for Sundays on November 6 and 13. Tickets are available online at www.ymtcbayarea.org or at the door one hour before curtain. Ticket prices are $16–$34, with discounts for students, seniors, military, teachers, and groups. The organization brings together the Bay Area’s most talented and dedicated young performers – as well as students of technical theater – with professional directors, designers, choreographers and musicians. They take on challenging and sophisticated musical and dramatic themes. Productions are always accompanied by a full, live orchestra. articles.text: Exhibit at Center for the Arts celebrates society’s 108th anniversary The California Society of Printmakers will be celebrating its 108th anniversary with an exhibit at the Piedmont Center for the Arts, with an opening reception on Friday, November 11 from 6:00 until 9:00 p.m. The exhibition features the work of more than 80 printmakers and highlights a wide variety of printmaking techniques, including serigraphs, monotypes, lithographs, etchings, woodcuts, and aquatints. The talented artists represent CSP members from throughout California. Some examples of the myriad of forms of printmaking you can see on display, include Oakland artist Luz Marina Ruiz, whose displayed work is a handmade artist Tunnel Book. Within the three-dimensional work, Luz incorporates linocuts embellished with watercolor and gouache on BFK paper. Another artist, Toru Sugita from Albany, depicts the changing or transitional monuments of the Bay Area using his own photographs and sketches of his surroundings to capture these spaces and textures through screen printing. Alicia Persaud, from Santa Roxanne Sexauer, Carnival Ostinato IV, Relief, Monoserigraph, Stencil, Chine Collé, BFK Rives, grey, 11.5” x 15.5”, 2022 Cruz, also creates work influenced by their environment. In her work on display she uses photo-intaglio with digital chine collé, to generate both sharp and blurred qualities layered together. She describes her process as, “depicting movement and motion of my memories both aesthetically through the imagery as well as emotionally through the physicality of the photo intaglio-process itself, highlighting how memories often blend together and change over time”. Some printmakers like Katherine Levin Lau from San Jose create images by hand painting on a zinc plate and then running the piece through the press many times. In Katherine’s detailed and dreamy scenes of nature, the original paintings are monochromatic. She enhances them with color layers using viscosity techniques. A final example of the breadth of techniques that will be on view is a work from Los Angeles artist Roxanne Sexauer, who utilizes a combination of printing methods including relief, monoserigraph, stencil, and chine collé to develop rich layers of abstract images. Only a small sampling of the unique work has been described here. articles.text: Review by Chris Honore’ Last Chance Harvey uses a familiar template that Hollywood has often turned to – estranged father attends daughter’s wedding and after a series of unexpected events, both comedic and dramatic, he finds redemption. What makes Harvey entertaining is not the story, but the fine performances of Dustin Hoffman and Emma Thompson. Both are charming and delightful to watch and raise this film to a new level by their sheer acting ability. They meet in a London bar. When they begin their hesitant, quasi-hostile dance of getting acquainted, they are so engaging it’s impossible not to conclude that Last Chance Harvey is very much a film that possesses a nice glow. At the outset, using deft parallel editing, we are introduced to Harvey Shine and Kate Walker and discover that they are both lonely people. Harvey has lost his job and seemingly his daughter, and Kate is convinced that she is defined by her age and seeming isolation. Without realizing it, they set out to prove others wrong. About so many things. Watching them interact, first as strangers and then as friends, is to observe two consummate actors who can look into the camera and with a look, a smile, a raise of the eyebrows say volumes. It males it hard to bid these two likable people adieu as the credits begin to roll. Last Chance Harvey. Directed by Joel Hopkins. Starring Dustin Hoffman, Emma Thompson, James Brolin and Kathy Baker. 1 hr., 32 min. Rated PG-13. Released 2009. Now Streaming on VUDU/Prime/Apple tv. articles.text: Almost Famous: Queen of Basketball is about Lucy Harris, arguably the greatest women’s basketball player. A free screening of two Academy Award winning shorts on Title IX, Queen of Basketball and Mink, will be shown on Thursday, November 3 at 7 p.m. at Ellen Driscoll Playhouse on the Havens School campus, 325 Highland Avenue. • Queen of Basketball Lucy Harris scored the first basket in Olympic women’s basketball and was drafted by the NBA. If not for Title IX, she couldn’t have gone to college and had either opportunity. In The Queen of Basketball, Lucy tells her own story, from being “too tall and that’s all” to finding her place in sports. The film won an Academy Award in 2022 as Best Short Documentary. • Mink! Ironically, TitIe IX almost didn’t pass because one of its key sponsors, Patsy Mink, was called away for a family emergency. Mink! tells the story of Rep. Patsy Mink’s path as the first woman of color to serve in Congress, and the crucial role she played in the passage of Title IX. The two films will be followed by a conversation with Chelle Putzer and Eva Phalen of the Piedmont Recreation Department. Masks are required. Mink! focuses on Patsy Takemoto Mink, the first woman of color elected to Congress. Title IX is the federal legislation that prohibits sex-based discrimination in any school or other education program that receives federal funding. articles.text: Mulberry’s switching to compostables Mulberry’s is going green. Piedmont’s popular, one-andonly market is now using compostable utensils and is “slowly transitioning” from plastic to compostable cups and deli containers. According to General Manager Sal Viveros, compostable utensils replaced plastic six weeks ago, and compostable cups and deli containers are on order. But, he said, “there’s a supply chain problem. We expect deli containers to arrive in three to four weeks, but the coffee cups may take three to four months.” Viveros estimates Mulberry’s uses a total of 1,000 coffee cups and deli containers a week. The costs for compostable, he says, are almost 35% to 40% higher than the costs of plastic, up from 18 to 25 cents per cup to 30 to 40 cents. “Right now, we’re absorbing the cost, but eventually, we’ll have to pass it on to customers,” he said. “Plastic clamshell containers used for takeout salads are harder to replace,” he said, “because it’s difficult to find a vendor. Eighty percent of the market’s straws are now compostable, except for slushies, which still use plastic because of vendor supply.” Mulberry’s leftover food that is still edible – breads, salads, sushi, anything that cannot be sold the next day – is picked up every day and donated to homeless shelters, schools and other organizations. The market uses Republic Services to recycle its bottles, cans and cardboard, and for composting its food waste. While Mulberry’s offers organic and non-organic products, many packaged goods on the store shelves still come wrapped in plastic. Viveros agrees with the City’s Mulberry’s Market General Manager Sal Viveros. Staff photo goal to have the market transition to 100 percent compostable and biodegradable materials. “It’s what I want to leave for my kids,” he said. He also credits the market’s barista, Jill Ohaviano, for encouraging the transition to compostable materials. “She’s been a tremendous help,” he said. “Eventually, probably a year from now, we will be 100 percent zero waste,” Viveros predicted. Alyssa Dykman, the city of Piedmont’s Sustainability Manager, is delighted with Mulberry’s transition. “I’m thrilled to see a Piedmont local business working to incorporate sustainability into their business practices,” she said, “as well as leveraging resources to reduce food waste and help address food insecurity. People often don’t realize how much food they throw away every day that could be eaten or repurposed. As the sole grocery store in Piedmont, Mulberry’s has an important role in the community.” Dykman notes that the City itself is striving to become more sustainable. “Last December, the Sustainable Procurement Policy was updated to minimize the City’s contribution to solid waste disposal, pollution and climate change through its purchases and practices. Since then “we’ve seen an increase in green waste materials collected and diverted from the landfill,” she added. Piedmont’s Sustainability Division also helps residents reduce their own carbon footprint through City sponsored programs such as the Piedmont Climate Challenge, the induction cooktop lending program, compost giveaways at the Corporation Yard, and an upcoming pilot program for home electrification rebates. articles.text: Dear Jim: I have noticed recently what looks like mold in the crawlspace under my home. What is causing this and how can I get rid of it? Is it possible that this could be causing health issues for me? I have noticed lately that I have had a lot of allergies and breathing issues I did not have before, and they seem to be getting worse over time. –Fred S. Mold is a common problem under Bay Area homes, and something I see frequently when I’m inspecting crawlspaces and basements. I’m not a mold expert, but the three most common types we see are black mold (most toxic), yellow or orange mold (house eating mold (fortunately rare), and white mold. White mold is fairly common, and fortunately, it is the least toxic of the three. It can still present problems for those with a chronic low-level exposure. Mold spores can infiltrate through floors and ductwork, and can make their way into livCrawlspace mold develops in moist soil due to lack of proper drainage. Black mold is more common in basement walls and bathrooms. ing spaces from down below. What causes this mold? Primarily it is drainage issues that have not been addressed, with water infiltrating through and under old foundations and getting into the dirt areas, and occasionally into walls and floor structures. Less frequently there are leaks in walls around poorly sealed windows and doors, siding or stucco, roofs etc., but it is mostly the subterranean moisture that is the culprit. You may also see a white substance on your foundations known as efflorescence. This is caused by water migrating through the concrete and depositing salts on the surface. Efflorescence is harmless, but it does indicate there are water issues that can lead to mold. There are a few different approaches to solve the problem. Some companies will put in plastic in the crawlspace to encapsulate the soil, along with other measures to control the humidity. From our perspective, this is not ideal as it doesn’t address the source of the problem and mold will continue to grow under the plastic. Proper drainage is the best first-line defense, consisting of French Drains and downspout drainage along with appropriate ventilation, keeping the water away from your building and improving air circulation. Over time these spaces will dry out and will no longer be breeding grounds for mold. We have had clients report back that their health issues have improved significantly after appropriate drainage is installed, which makes us believe we are on the right track. articles.text: The Wednesday walkers on October 19 included Jennifer Peltzer, Helene Farber, Pat Keller, Jasmine Cai, Fangfang Lai, Winston Lee, Melba Chen, Christine Calliste, Judith Lee, Adrienne Hamlin, Rob Smith, Quincy Dong, Laura Goldman, Phil Witte, Marion Lim Yankowitz, Jim Kuo, Carole Lyons, Mark Davis, Brenda Ferrero, Peter Persoff, Helen Dong, Stella Houston, Cheryl Coleman Jones, Ann Quinby, Lisa Euphrat, Nancy DeRoche with K-9 best friend Chili, Judy Wang, Mary Hedley, Kat Lang, Ian Morgan, Jim Kellogg, Nadine Guffanti, Elizabeth Richter, Dave DeRoche, Sarah Johnson, Priscilla Wanerus, Mike Gallant, Karin Fetherston, and Dick Carter. The group was pleased that Fangfang Lai brought her neighbor, Natalie Nussbaum, to walk with the group for the first time. A warm, sunny Wednesday last week may have encouraged a large gathering of 43 walkers and one K-9 best friend to participate in the weekly Walking on Wednesdays. One street the group hadn’t visited in a long time was Littlewood Drive, and going there offered the opportunity to share Piedmont Historical Society president Gail Lombardi’s history of Piedmont’s first and probably last manufacturing industry, silk fiber production. Going up Mountain Avenue they passed front yards ready for Halloween with scary house decorations, and one flying a Ukrainian flag. The long line of walkers stopped in the shade where Caperton Avenue runs into Mountain. This spot also gave them the opportunity to look around and see in a front yard a larger than life statue of a distinguished looking gentleman dressed in what looks like a suit made of leaves. The walkers continued their climb on Mountain to Dudley Avenue, and then up to Littlewood. As group photo was taken, Gail Lombardi’s Piedmont silk farm history was told. At the end the end of the 19th century there were only three types of cloth, cotton, wool and silk. The U.S. government thought silk could be produced in America, and funded groups to create experimental silk producing stations. It was believed that silk production could provide employment for women, reduce unemployment, and increase family income. In the early 1880s the Ladies’ Silk Culture Society purchased 15 acres of land at the top and eastern side of Mountain Avenue, where Dudley and Littlewood Avenues are today. The society planted mulberry trees, whose leaves are the principal food of silk worms, and built a two-story, eight-room cocoonery. The locals called it the “Silk Farm.” The trees and this history provided the inspiration for the name of today’s Mulberry’s Market. By 1885 the grove was thriving, and an additional seven acres were purchased. About 100 women were employed. During their lives, silkworms consume 50 times their weight in mulberry leaves. The women harvested and chopped them and fed them to the worms in trays four times a day. The worms reached maturity in 35 days and spun their cocoons. At the Silk Farm the cocoons were fumigated to kill the pupa, softened in hot water, and unreeled as separate silken fibers. One cocoon could produce a continuous silk filament up to 300 feet long, almost the length of a football field. Several filaments were spun together to form one silk thread. Natalie Nussbaum and Fangfang Lai said they had visited silk farms on trips to China. The Silk Farm in Piedmont didn’t prosper. The canyon was not warm enough for the worms and the women would not work for less than a dollar a day, while Chinese workers were only paid six cents a day. So, in 1895 the farm closed. The group of walkers descended own Littlewood and its canyon to where the Silk Farm’s mulberry trees had been planted, however no trees survived. The walkers came to the dead-end of Littlewood, but a long driveway continues on. Just before a home’s large gate at the driveway’s end is a surprising, old, red, London telephone booth. Some members of the group had seen it on past visits, but there was still no explanation of how it got there. The group then began tracing its steps and made the climb back up Littlewood. Returning the city center it was all downhill. It had gotten warm, and the walkers were pleased to be returning to the Exedra. For a variety they visited Poplar Way, which doesn’t seem to have any poplar trees, and then on to Lakeview, Sheridan, and Highland Avenue. The two-mile walk was completed in a little over an hour. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group and there is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome. Registration with the Piedmont Recreation Department is required at https:// tinyurl.com/3ethkehu. pages.text: Wednesday, October 26, 2022 25 Walking on Wednesday Wednesday Walkers discover Piedmont’s early silk worm factory The Wednesday walkers on October 19 included Jennifer Peltzer, Helene Farber, Pat Keller, Jasmine Cai, Fangfang Lai, Winston Lee, Melba Chen, Christine Calliste, Judith Lee, Adrienne Hamlin, Rob Smith, Quincy Dong, Laura Goldman, Phil Witte, Marion Lim Yankowitz, Jim Kuo, Carole Lyons, Mark Davis, Brenda Ferrero, Peter Persoff, Helen Dong, Stella Houston, Cheryl Coleman Jones, Ann Quinby, Lisa Euphrat, Nancy DeRoche with K-9 best friend Chili, Judy Wang, Mary Hedley, Kat Lang, Ian Morgan, Jim Kellogg, Nadine Guffanti, Elizabeth Richter, Dave DeRoche, Sarah Johnson, Priscilla Wanerus, Mike Gallant, Karin Fetherston, and Dick Carter. The group was pleased that Fangfang Lai brought her neighbor, Natalie Nussbaum, to walk with the group for the first time. By Dick Carter A warm, sunny Wednesday last week may have encouraged a large gathering of 43 walkers and one K-9 best friend to participate in the weekly Walking on Wednesdays. One street the group hadn’t visited in a long time was Littlewood Drive, and going there offered the opportunity to share Piedmont Historical Society president Gail Lombardi’s history of Piedmont’s first and probably last manufacturing industry, silk fiber production. Going up Mountain Avenue they passed front yards ready for Halloween with scary house decorations, and one flying a Ukrainian flag. The long line of walkers stopped in the shade where Caperton Avenue runs into Mountain. This spot also gave them the opportunity to look around and see in a front yard a larger than life statue of a distinguished looking gentleman dressed in what looks like a suit made of leaves. The walkers continued their climb on Mountain to Dudley Avenue, and then up to Littlewood. As group photo was taken, Gail Lombardi’s Piedmont silk farm history was told. At the end the end of the 19th century there were only three types of cloth, cotton, wool and silk. The U.S. government thought silk could be produced in America, and funded groups to create experimental silk producing stations. It was believed that silk production could provide employment for women, reduce unemployment, and increase family income. In the early 1880s the Ladies’ Silk Culture Society purchased 15 acres of land at the top and eastern side of Mountain Avenue, where Dudley and Littlewood Avenues are today. The society planted mulberry trees, whose leaves are the principal food of silk worms, and built a two-story, eight-room cocoonery. The locals called it the “Silk Farm.” The trees and this history provided the inspiration for the name of today’s Mulberry’s Market. By 1885 the grove was thriving, and an additional seven acres were purchased. About 100 women were employed. During their lives, silkworms consume 50 times their weight in mulberry leaves. The women harvested and chopped them and fed them to the worms in trays four times a day. The worms reached maturity in 35 days and spun their cocoons. At the Silk Farm the cocoons were fumigated to kill the pupa, softened in hot water, and unreeled as separate silken fibers. One cocoon could produce a continuous silk filament up to 300 feet long, almost the length of a football field. Several filaments were spun together to form one silk thread. Natalie Nussbaum and Fangfang Lai said they had visited silk farms on trips to China. The Silk Farm in Piedmont didn’t prosper. The canyon was not warm enough for the worms and the women would not work for less than a dollar a day, while Chinese workers were only paid six cents a day. So, in 1895 the farm closed. The group of walkers descended own Littlewood and its canyon to where the Silk Farm’s mulberry trees had been planted, however no trees survived. The walkers came to the dead-end of Littlewood, but a long driveway continues on. Just before a home’s large gate at the driveway’s end is a surprising, old, red, London telephone booth. Some members of the group had seen it on past visits, but there was still no explanation of how it got there. The group then began tracing its steps and made the climb back up Littlewood. Returning the city center it was all downhill. It had gotten warm, and the walkers were pleased to be returning to the Exedra. For a variety they visited Poplar Way, which doesn’t seem to have any poplar trees, and then on to Lakeview, Sheridan, and Highland Avenue. The two-mile walk was completed in a little over an hour. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group and there is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome. Registration with the Piedmont Recreation Department is required at https:// tinyurl.com/3ethkehu. Upon moving in, Ruchi got right to work, helping to organize our neighborhood Fourth of July block party…and she just kept going. While balancing a busy professional life and a growing family, she stepped up to volunteer for the three-year commitment as Beach Parents Organization Vice President and then President. She took on her pandemic-era presidency as a growth opportunity, leading to a hybrid-based approach to community building, and finding creative ways to ease the isolation for both kids and parents. She was able to adjust the role and processes of the BPO to fit our circumstances, intuitively knowing what to prioritize. Her contributions to the BPO, will endure. Ruchi’s character is perfectly suited for a position on the School Board. A scientist by training, she is thoughtful and analytical in her approach to problems. We never hear he complain about an issue; instead, she sets her mind at work to figuring out the problem and then fixing it. We have witnessed her unflappable patience on many occasions, whether it pertains to home, school, or community, and have also marveled at her ability to be able to talk to anyone about a diverse variety of issues. Ruchi believes that a strong sense of belonging, in concert with a high standard of academic excellence, will lift up all of our students. And knowing Ruchi, she’ll still have time for our neighborhood block party in July. Please vote for Ruchi in November. –Leila Hebshi (BPO President 2018-2019) and Peter Udovch

articles.text: Editor: When I met Jen Long three years ago, I soon realized that we had more than a few things in common. Neither of us was a California native. We had each moved to Piedmont around the same time and felt welcomed here. Our teenage children, back then, were both high school sophomores. As I got to know Jen better, though, it became clear she was a kindred spirit. She values community service and working to address unmet needs. She is an upstander who leans into civic engagement. She sees the promise and potential of an inclusive Piedmont and is willing to do the necessary work to get us there. Jen won unanimous support when she was appointed to fill a vacant seat on City Council earlier this year. That’s not surprising because she connects easily with others in social and civic leadership spaces. I saw this when Jen partnered with young leaders from Piedmont Middle School to lead a community march. I saw it when she stepped up to serve as co-president of the Piedmont Anti-Racism and Diversity Committee and hit the ground running with popular new programming. articles.text: At 4:17 a.m. on Thursday, October 20, Piedmont Police were notified of the first of four fires that morning believed to have been started by one arsonist. One trash can, a stack of wooden pallets and two different Halloween scarecrows were set on fire. The suspect remains at large. The first call was for a trash can in flames on Grand Avenue in Oakland, which was extinguished by the police. Minutes later at 4:21 a.m. patrolling officers observed multiple wooden pallets on fire in the Ace Hardware parking lot on Grand Avenue. Officers immediately notified the fire department and worked to put the fire out with fire extinguishers to prevent the flames from spreading. “Just before 4:30 a.m., I noticed light flickering on my bedroom windows,” said resident Don Dare of nearby Wildwood Avenue. “I looked out the window to see a raging fire at least 15 feet tall with sparks flying high into the night sky.” Officers were able to extinguish the fire and were later assisted by the Piedmont Fire Department to confirm the fire was out. Later in the morning, Halloween decorations were lit on Photo of a suspect in four arson fires on October 20. fire in the 300 block of Wildwood Avenue and the 100 block of Sierra Avenue. At both sites a scarecrow was set on fire. Police received notification of the Wildwood Avenue fire at 6:55 a.m. and at 7:20 a.m. on Sierra Avenue. The resident on Sierra was able to extinguish the fire himself. Minimal property damage was reported. The photo of a suspect was captured on video at the involved locations. Residents who have any information related to this or video of unusual activity related to the events are asked to contact the Piedmont Police Department at (510) 420-3000. Pallets burn in the Ace Hardware parking lot at 4:30 a.m. on Thursday, October 20.
